gap: No result ChatGPT got states on a common basis how long the battery lasts or what the watt rating means for the speakers it showed. Avantree advertises the $99.99 PowerByte as '30W' with '20hr' playtime, and Target lists the $31.99 iHome iBT330 at 'up to 30 hours'. Neither gives a volume, a radio-or-Bluetooth mode, or says whether the watts are RMS or peak, so these figures can't be ranked against each other.
standout_why: I compared against itechguides 'Best Bluetooth Speakers with FM Radio: 3 Top Picks', rottenwifi 'Best Bluetooth Speakers With FM Radio in 2026' and powersof10 'Best Bluetooth Speakers with Radio 2026'. None of them works out runtime per volume level or per mode, and none says whether watts are RMS or peak for the products ChatGPT showed (PowerByte, iBT330, BoomByte, SP850, Tivoli Model One BT). But the problem itself is already on those pages. Rottenwifi warns against ranking 'sound by wattage alone', and powersof10 says 'Manufacturers' battery claims assume 50% volume'. Powersof10 also gives the SP850 only as '3W' with 'Variable battery life'. The new piece would be Avantree's own figure tied to a volume level (17 h at 60% volume for the PowerByte, 6 h at medium volume for the SP850). I couldn't open those pages to confirm it, so the finding I can actually stand behind adds only part of what's missing.
decides: So far this only confirms that the pick can't be made on the advertised numbers. ChatGPT's 'best for powerful sound' (PowerByte, 30W, 20 h) and 'best outdoor' (iBT330, 30 h) cards rest on watt and hour figures with no conditions attached. If the Avantree figures tied to volume levels can be sourced, the SP850 would drop out as an all-day pick: its 6 h at medium volume would be about a third of the PowerByte's 17 h at 60% volume. The iBT330's 30 h would need its own condition before it could be called the longest-lasting.
